channel.title: iRecord Updates
channel.description: Updates for iRecord - Professional screen recording

item.title: Version 1.222.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.222.0

Fixed

  • Saving a long recording no longer fails with "Cannot Decode" — past a certain length, saving stopped partway and reported two words that explained nothing. Your recording was never damaged: the app was decoding your footage several times over at once — once to save it, and again to keep the preview and the camera running behind the Save screen — while holding on to frames it had finished with. macOS eventually shut the decoder down, which the app reported as being unable to read your video. It now stops the preview while saving and releases frames as it uses them. This was never about a particular Mac; it reproduced on one with twice the memory. Saving also got faster: the shape used to round the camera's corners was being redrawn for every frame instead of once, and the progress bar was being updated fifty thousand times.
  • A save that loses frames says so — if a Mac ran short of memory mid-save, frames could be dropped and the video would come out shorter than the canvas with nothing said about it. That can no longer pass in silence.
  • The preview stops when a save starts — it used to keep playing, and keep decoding the same footage, for the whole export.

Changed

  • A failed update now leaves evidence behind — when an update would not install, nothing was written down anywhere, so the only account of it was the customer's memory of a dialog. Sparkle's download, install and failure steps now go into the app's log, naming the reason the way the developers of Sparkle name it rather than as a bare number, and a diagnostics report picks them up. The report also says where iRecord is installed and whether it can update itself from there — an app still running from its disk image, or from a copy macOS has quarantined, cannot replace itself no matter how many times you check for updates, and neither state looks wrong from the outside. Drag iRecord to Applications and it can.

item.title: Version 1.221.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.221.0

Changed

  • The timeline zooms out to the whole recording, and in to a single frame — a long recording could not be seen end to end at any zoom, and could not be zoomed in far enough to place a cut on a frame. The zoom-out end now means "everything, in one screen", whatever the recording's length, and the zoom-in end reaches frame level. The editor opens showing the whole thing, Fit returns to it in one click, the two magnifiers step in and out, and zooming keeps the playhead where your eye already is instead of scrolling out from under you. Long timelines also stay smooth while you do it.
  • Picking a window tells you what each window is — the grid was ragged, and windows that could not be previewed all came out as the same grey rectangle, so four different windows read as one app repeated. Every window now shows its app icon — instead of the preview when there isn't one, beside it when there is — with the window title and the app it belongs to on every card. A line under the grid explains what the list contains: windows from every desktop and Space, which is why some have no preview and all of them are still recordable.
  • The camera's Fine-tune settings are easier to find, and easier to skip — the row that opens position, size, shape and border was the faintest thing in the panel while being the door to all of it. It now reads as a control, and when closed it shows what it is hiding, so checking your framing costs nothing.
  • A new recording's camera has no white ring — the border was 2 px by default, a styling opinion applied to footage nobody had looked at yet. It now starts at 0 and the slider is there when you want one. Recordings you have already made are untouched.
  • Reporting a problem now brings the evidence with it — Help → "Report an Issue…" gathers a diagnostics file, shows it to you in Finder, and opens an email ready to send. Attach the file and the report arrives with your macOS version, Mac model, free disk space, permission states and the app's own log, instead of "it didn't work". Nothing is sent anywhere on its own: the file is written to your Mac, you read it, and you decide whether to attach it. It contains no video and no licence key.

Fixed

  • A failed save says where it failed — an export that could not read part of a recording reported two words, "Cannot Decode", with no indication of what had gone wrong or where. It now names the point in the video it stopped at, so a damaged stretch of one take is identifiable instead of looking like a broken app.

item.title: Version 1.220.1
item.description:
What's New in 1.220.1

Fixed

  • A trimmed-down clip can always be dragged back out — trim a section short enough and Record next section came to rest on top of it, covering the very handle you needed to undo the trim. The button now starts after the last block instead of after the timeline's nominal end, and a trim can no longer shrink a block below the width it is drawn at, so the state that trapped the clip cannot be reached in the first place. Zoom in when you need to trim finer than the lane can show.

item.title: Version 1.220.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.220.0

Fixed

  • Trimming a clip no longer overshoots — dragging a clip's end moved it many times further than the cursor went, so the first edit most people try collapsed the clip instead of shortening it. A 40-pixel drag now trims exactly what 40 pixels is worth, and the handle stays under the cursor for the whole drag, in both directions.
  • Re-recording a section keeps the edits you made in it — if you had split a section into three and then re-recorded it, all three pieces were silently thrown away and ⌘Z could not bring them back. Your splits and trims now carry across to the new take, because they are positions in the section, not in one particular file. When a take is genuinely too short to hold them, the app says so and how much shorter it is, rather than quietly rearranging the timeline. Re-recording is a single ⌘Z away either way.

Added

  • A clip's ends look draggable — the trim handles were invisible until you happened to hover exactly over them. Each end now carries a quiet grip at rest, turns amber under the pointer, and marks the exact cut while you drag. The area you can grab is twice as wide as the handle you see.
  • Every take you record is reachable — a section that has been re-recorded shows ⟲ 3 on its timeline block, listing each take with its length so you can put an earlier one back. Nothing was ever deleted; until now there was simply no way to get to it.
  • Clip lengths show tenths under a minute — the sliver left by a split used to read "0:00".

Changed

  • The timeline says what an edit cost — when a re-recorded take is too short to hold the splits you had made, a line above the timeline says how much shorter it is and what no longer applies, instead of quietly rearranging the blocks.

item.title: Version 1.219.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.219.0

  • Every section can have its own camera view — a recording no longer has to look the same the whole way through. Set the intro to **Camera full**, the demo to **Corner**, the wrap-up to **Side by side**, and the video cuts between them at the section boundaries, in the editor canvas and in the saved MP4 alike. Switch the Camera panel from *Whole recording* to *Each section*, then move the playhead to the section you want to reframe; the timeline shows each block's framing so you can read the cuts at a glance. Flipping the switch either way never changes what is on screen — turning it on gives every section the look the recording already had, and turning it off keeps the one you are looking at.
  • A "Camera full" view — the camera alone, filling the frame. The talking-head shot an intro or a sign-off wants, and the thing that made every other framing feel like a variation on one layout.
  • A section recorded without the camera could show the previous section's frozen face — the exported video held the last camera frame it had seen across any section that had no camera of its own. Those sections now play with no camera, which is what they were recorded as.
  • Camera framing is chosen, not assembled — the Camera panel used to spend three controls on one decision: a checkbox to enable the camera, a picker to choose a mode, and a stack of sliders to place it. It is now a row of four swatches that draw the layout they produce — **Screen only**, **Corner**, **Side by side**, **Camera full** — and the numbers moved behind *Fine-tune* for the rare time you want 27% rather than 25%. Nothing was taken away: every slider is still there, and switching views and back returns the framing you tuned rather than a factory default.
  • The app is now called iRecord — same app, the name it ships under at irecord.video. Direktor was the internal working name and is retired; earlier entries in this file keep it because that is what those releases were called.
  • The bundle identifier moved to `com.irecord.app` (from `com.direktor.app`).
  • Your Recordings moved from `~/Movies/Direktor` to `~/Movies/iRecord` — migrated automatically the first time the renamed app launches, once. Nothing is copied twice and nothing is left behind; if the new folder already exists the migration is skipped.
  • Version numbers now read `1.219.0` — major, the day of the year, and a counter for repeat releases on the same day. The same scheme the Expo apps use. Earlier entries in this file keep their `YYYY.MM.DD` headings because that is genuinely what those builds were called.
  • iRecord requires macOS 15 (Sequoia) and an Apple Silicon Mac. Microphone capture is a macOS 15 API with no earlier equivalent, so on macOS 14 the app recorded your screen and your Mac's own sound but silently dropped your voice — the kind of failure you only discover after the take. Rather than ship that, the app now says it needs Sequoia. Apple Silicon is the same principle applied to hardware: it is what can actually be tested, and an Intel build nobody could debug would be a worse promise than an honest limit.
